answer.evidence: Rows 0-34 form a long, light, speckled top surface of the wall, with a few notches. Row 35 is a bright 1-row front-edge line (L=189) and row 36 is a lighter step (L=163). Below them, rows 37-43 are a darker south end face (L about 120), and rows 44-46 are a dark base. The face is 7 rows, or about 10 with the base, so it is well over 3 rows. The dark vertical strips at the left and right edges are outlines, not receding side faces. The top surface is clearly drawn with an edge line above a distinct front face, so it reads as three-quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, one-tile-wide wall strip, so it is judged by eye as a sparse object. Its measured 9 visible tones per tile are close to the references' 10 and 12. Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as the references. Only 1% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so the edges are tinted (dark grey-green/brown) rather than a black sticker line. The top face shows about 5 grey steps with speckle, notches and a moss touch at the south end, and the end face is darker for value separation. It is less varied than the stone and roof surfaces of the references (18 distinct colours in total against 66 and 185), which makes it slightly lower in density. It still reads as shaded, textured concrete, not a flat fill.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, sparse wall strip, so I judged it by eye against the house references and used the measured facts as support. It has 9 visible tones per full tile, against 12 for house-h101_0 and 10 for house-h112_0-stone, so it is close to the references. Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references, so there are no flat fills. Only 1% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, so the edges carry a tint and read as dark material tone rather than a black sticker line. Overall it is slightly lower in density and has one fewer shading step, but a careful artist would accept it next to the references without it looking flat or sticker-like.
